text:
[natalie] There it is. Careful, the dish is still hot — Amy, honey, pass me that towel. Third try's the charm on this bread, I'm telling you. First loaf came out a brick, second one a sponge, and this one — well, look at it. This one came out a loaf of bread.

[amy] It smells incredible. Okay, I'm cutting into it, I don't care if it's supposed to rest.

[natalie] Bread doesn't need to rest, sugar, that's steak. Bread needs to be eaten while the butter still has an opinion about it.

[zadi] That's the best thing anyone has said at this table all year, and I include the night we argued about Middlemarch until one in the morning.

[amy] We didn't argue about Middlemarch. You argued about Middlemarch. I fell asleep on the couch and you kept going.

[zadi] And I was very persuasive, you said so yourself the next morning. Oh — this bread. Natalie. This bread is a whole event.

[natalie] It's my grandmother's recipe, out of the little tin box, the one with the rooster on it. Half the cards in there are just lists of things with no instructions at all. Flour, buttermilk, the good honey, patience. That's the whole card. Took me three loaves to figure out what patience meant in her handwriting.

[amy] It means the oven was slower in her day, probably.

[natalie] That's exactly what it means. I gave it an extra quarter hour at a lower heat and there she was, like her hand was on my shoulder the whole time.

[zadi] I finished the Robin McKinley last night, by the way. The one I've been carrying around for two weeks like a small pet.

[natalie] The dragon one?

[zadi] The dragon one. And the ending — I'm not going to spoil it, but I closed the book and just sat there holding it for a while. The way she lands it. It's like watching someone set a full cup down without a single ripple. I went back and read the last page twice just to feel it land again.

[amy] Two weeks is fast for you with a book you like. You usually ration them.

[zadi] I do ration them. I failed. It was too good, I have no regrets, and now I get the other kind of pleasure, which is choosing the next one. I've got three on the shelf making their cases.

[natalie] Let them audition. Make them bring something to the table. Speaking of which — the tomatoes in the salad are mine, I want that on the record. First real bowlful off those vines.

[amy] Wait, these? The ones you were nursing along in June like they were in intensive care?

[natalie] Those exact ones. They turned the corner. I gave them the sunny bed by the fence, talked to them scandalous, and look — they went and got delicious about it.

[zadi] They really did. This whole salad tastes like July did its job.

[amy] Oh, I have to tell you both — I spent Sunday in the pantry with the radio on, and it was honestly the nicest afternoon I've had in weeks. Everything's in jars now. I opened the door this morning just to stand there and look at it.

[natalie] Oh, that's the best feeling. Shelves you can trust.

[amy] And I found three cans of the same beans hiding behind everything, which is where the bean salad came from. So thank the pantry for tonight's contribution.

[zadi] A dish with a backstory. Those always taste better, I'm convinced of it.

[natalie] Every good table is nothing but backstories, sugar. That's the recipe box again. Cobbler's coming out in a minute — peaches from the stand out on the county road, the one with the dog that supervises the till.

[amy] The one where the dog sits on the stool like an employee?

[natalie] Like middle management, yes. I bought two baskets and he approved the transaction personally.

[zadi] I love that dog. Someone should write him into a novel. A small, honest novel where nothing bad happens and the peaches are always ripe.

[natalie] Well, tonight's chapter of it is in the oven. Y'all save room.

[amy] I saved room. I planned for cobbler the way I plan everything — in advance and with contingencies.

[zadi] She means she skipped lunch.

[amy] I mean I had a strategic lunch.

[natalie] Here we go — oh, it's pretty. Look at that crust. Get the cream, it's in the blue pitcher.

[zadi] Oh. Oh, that's — everyone stop talking for a second. This deserves quiet.

[amy] Mm.

[natalie] Mm-hmm. That's the county-road peaches doing that. You can't buy that in a store, that's a dog-supervised peach.

[zadi] This is the part of the evening I like best, you know. Not the cobbler — well, also the cobbler. But this part. Candles getting low, nobody in a hurry. The conversation starts taking its shoes off.

[amy] The week can just sit down somewhere, it's off duty.

[natalie] That's what a table's for, sugar. You cook the dinner so the evening has somewhere soft to land.

[zadi] Next month it's my table, and fair warning, I cook one thing well and it's soup. There will be soup, there will be bread I bought from someone more talented than me, and there will be a poem before anyone's allowed to leave. A short one. Traditional.

[natalie] I wouldn't miss it. I'll bring the honey, the good kind, for the bread.

[amy] I'll bring the labels, in case your pantry wants to become trustworthy while we're there.

[zadi] My pantry is beyond your help, but you're welcome to try. Is there more of the decaf?

[natalie] Pot's still warm. Sit, I'll get it. No — sit. Hosting means I get to say that.

[amy] The candles are almost down to the wood. I always like when they get like this.

[zadi] Mm. Everything's gone all amber.

[natalie] That's the hour doing that. Best light of the whole day, right here at the end of it. Nothing left to do but sit in it a while.

[zadi] Mm-hmm.

[amy] Mm.

[natalie] More cream in that, honey? There. Now we're all where we're supposed to be.

[zadi] Sit, sit — it's soup, it doesn't need a standing ovation. That's the whole menu, I told everybody. Soup, and bread I didn't make.

[natalie] I'm not sitting, I'm looking. That is not just soup. What'd you put in it?

[zadi] I don't know. Leeks. The recipe knew. I just did what it said.

[amy] Where do you want the bread, on the—

[zadi] The board's fine. No — the other board. Yeah, there.

[natalie] I brought the honey. Said I would.

[zadi] You did say.

[natalie] For the bread. Not the soup. Nobody put the honey in the soup.

[zadi] Why would I put honey in the soup.

[amy] You might've.

[zadi] I would not have.

[amy] I brought the labels, too.

[zadi] Course you did.

[amy] Just in case.

[zadi] My pantry doesn't want to be trustworthy, Amy. It likes keeping a couple of secrets.

[amy] It had two open bags of flour last time. Same flour.

[zadi] That's not a secret. That's a surplus.

[natalie] Y'all. This is good. Zadi. This is actually good.

[zadi] Is it?

[natalie] Don't do that. You know it is.

[zadi] I hoped. You can't tell with soup till somebody else eats it.

[amy] It's good.

[zadi] Okay. Good.

[natalie] Let me get the — where's your ladle—

[zadi] Sit.

[natalie] I'm only reaching, honey, you're all the way over there—

[zadi] Nope. My table. I get to say it. Sit.

[natalie] Well, now. Would you look at that.

[amy] She's been saving that a whole month.

[zadi] A month exactly. Since your table. I wrote it down.

[natalie] You did not write it down.

[zadi] Mentally.

[natalie] Mm-hmm. Pass the honey, then, boss.

[zadi] Here. It's yours, you brought it, you know how it goes.

[natalie] It's from the man out past the feed store. Keeps his hives back behind the tree line. Doesn't label a thing — you point at a jar and he tells you what field it came off of.

[zadi] What field's this one.

[natalie] Clover, he said. Late clover. I couldn't tell you clover from anything, but I believed him.

[amy] He should label them.

[natalie] He should not. Half the point is the man telling you.

[amy] I could bring him some labels.

[zadi] Do not bring that man labels.

[natalie] Leave him be. He's happy back there.

[natalie] Look at that on the warm bread, though. Runny in the good way.

[amy] Store bread holds honey tighter. Doesn't soak.

[natalie] Whose is it? The bread.

[zadi] The corner place. The one with the — you know the one.

[natalie] The sourdough in the window.

[zadi] That one. I'm not proud. I know my one thing, and it's soup.

[amy] Knowing your one thing is underrated.

[zadi] See, that's nice. Write that down.

[amy] I don't write things down.

[natalie] She doesn't. She just remembers everything. It's a little unsettling.

[zadi] It's my aunt's, the recipe. She only ever made it for people she liked, so I felt very chosen, growing up, getting a bowl.

[natalie] That's the best kind of soup there is.

[zadi] I called her to get it right and all she'd say was, you'll know. Very helpful.

[natalie] That's my grandmother's cards exactly. You'll know.

[zadi] And do you? Ever?

[natalie] Eventually. After the brick, and the sponge — sure.

[zadi] I picked my next book, by the way.

[natalie] Oh, the audition's over.

[zadi] Finally, yeah. One of them wore me down.

[amy] Which one.

[zadi] The blue one. I don't even know what it's about. I liked the weight of it in my hand.

[natalie] You pick books like produce.

[zadi] I pick everything like produce. Squeeze it, smell it, trust it.

[amy] That explains the pantry.

[zadi] Leave my pantry out of it. You're a guest.

[amy] Whose month is it next.

[natalie] That's you, isn't it. We did mine, then Zadi's—

[amy] It's me. I've been ready since spring.

[natalie] Course you have.

[zadi] We'll all be using coasters.

[amy] You will be using coasters.

[natalie] She's got a diagram made up already, I'd put money on it.

[amy] There's a diagram. There's a whole plan.

[amy] More soup, while it's hot? Anybody.

[zadi] Half. Little bit.

[natalie] I'm slowing down. Started strong.

[amy] You went in hard on the bread.

[natalie] I did. I'd do it again.

[zadi] There's more if the regret shows up later.

[natalie] Oh, it always shows up later. That's what later's for.

[natalie] My tomatoes are done, by the way. Pulled the last of them this week.

[zadi] The intensive-care tomatoes.

[natalie] They pulled through, and then they quit. Like anybody does. I've got greens going in now.

[amy] Already?

[natalie] Cool-weather things. Something to fuss over through the fall.

[zadi] You just like having somebody out there to talk to.

[natalie] I like having something that listens. No offense.

[amy] None taken. I wasn't listening.

[zadi] Is this thyme, in the soup?

[amy] I was about to ask that.

[zadi] It came in a bundle. I used the bundle.

[amy] The whole bundle.

[zadi] I don't measure herbs, Amy. I'm not a chemist.

[amy] I measure herbs.

[zadi] I know you do. It shows. Yours always come out even.

[natalie] Candles are getting low.

[zadi] Mm. Let them.

[natalie] I like them like this. Down to that last steady bit.

[zadi] The part that's just glow.

[amy] Mm.

[zadi] Oh — the poem. Before anybody leaves. I promised a poem and I'm not letting it slide.

[natalie] You did promise a poem.

[amy] A short one, you said.

[zadi] It's short. Traditional — it's off my grandmother's side. Hang on. How's it start. Something, something — the day is done.

[natalie] Take your time, sugar.

[zadi] No, I've got it. "The day is done and wants for nothing. The bread is cut, the lamp is low. The last of the light goes soft and blue" — and the evening — "and the evening keeps the door."

[natalie] Oh. That's a nice one.

[amy] Mm. I like that.

[natalie] That's a good one to have by heart.

[zadi] It's the only one I've got by heart. That's how it got the job.

[natalie] There's a heel of bread nobody's claimed.

[amy] Not me. I'm done, and happily.

[zadi] It'll keep. Somebody's breakfast.

[natalie] Should I put the lid back on your honey?

[zadi] No — I like knowing it's there.

[amy] Mm.

[zadi] I'm not moving for a while. Sitting right here.

[natalie] Sit as long as you want. It's your table.

[zadi] Mm-hmm. So it is.

[amy] Whole room's gone amber.

[zadi] It does that, this hour.

[natalie] Mm.

[zadi] Leave the candles, I'll get them.

[natalie] In a minute.

[zadi] In a minute.

The stew had been on since noon, and by the time Amy and Zadi came in out of the cold it had cooked down to the thick part, where the potatoes gave up their edges and went soft into the rest of it. She kept it on a low flame while they hung their coats by the door. The kitchen was the warmest room in the house now that the evenings had turned. The window over the sink had gone dark early, and when she looked up from the pot she could see the three of them in it, small and lit.

"It smells like the whole house already ate," Zadi said, and sat down without being told.

Natalie set the bread out, her own this time, though she didn't say so and nobody asked. There was cornbread too, in the pan, still warm enough to matter. Amy had brought a jar of pickled beans and put it in the middle of the table where everyone could reach it.

They ate for a while without talking much. Natalie put seconds in the bowls before they were empty, and nobody stopped her. The stew was good. She could tell a few spoonfuls in, once she'd stopped checking it and started just eating it. She'd made too much again. There would be bowls to send home with both of them, and she'd set the containers out on the counter by the door before they came.

The pickled beans went fast. Amy reached in for the last of them before anyone else could, and nobody minded.

"This is exactly right for tonight," Amy said. "It's cold enough out there to mean it now."

"It came in fast this week," Natalie said. "One morning the porch was cold and that was that."

"I finished the blue book," Zadi said. She had it with her, on the chair at her side, the way she carried the ones she was still inside of. "It wasn't what I thought. I thought it was going to be sad, and it kept not being sad. I kept waiting for it."

"And?" Natalie said.

"And then it ended, and I was glad, and I felt a little tricked, in a good way." Zadi turned her spoon over.

"What was it about?" Natalie said.

"A house, mostly. A family that kept losing it and getting it back. It sounds like nothing when I say it, but it wasn't nothing. And now I've got nothing lined up to read. First time in a while."

"You'll find one," Amy said. "You always do."

"The shelf could run out."

"The shelf is not going to run out," Amy said, and that was the end of it.

Natalie got up to move the coffee off the heat and stood a moment at the counter with her back to them. Amy was saying something about next month, about her own table. She had already worked out where everyone would sit, and what she would make, and the order it would come out of the kitchen. There was a diagram, apparently. Zadi was laughing at her, gently, and Amy was letting her.

"You can laugh," Amy said. "You'll eat in the right order and you'll like it."

"I don't mind being told where to sit," Zadi said. "Saves me deciding."

Natalie brought the coffee to the table. The tomato jars from the end of summer were still going; she'd sent them home with everybody and kept a shelf of her own. The greens she'd put in were up now, low and dark, taking the cold better than she'd thought they would. She told them that part. Neither of them minded that it wasn't much of a story.

"Mine took," Amy said. "The little ones, by the back step where I can see them from the sink."

"Course you do," Natalie said.

Zadi buttered a corner of the cornbread and ate it slowly while the others talked.

The honey was still on the table from the bread, the clover kind from the man past the feed store, the jar not quite closed. Zadi reached over and pressed the lid down without being asked, and went back to her coffee.

The coffee had come out strong and nobody said anything about it. Zadi held her cup in both hands. The lamp on the sideboard was the only light now besides the low one over the stove, and it put a soft yellow across the table and left the corners of the room alone. Natalie didn't get up to change it. The room stayed that size, this late, pulled in close around the three of them and what was left on the plates.

Amy started stacking the bowls, and Natalie told her to leave them, and for once Amy left them. She set the top bowl back down and put her hands in her lap. The stack stood there in the middle of the table, unfinished, and that was fine.

Outside, the wind had come up a little, and the house made its small sound somewhere up above them, and nothing else. The candle in front of Natalie had burned down nearly to the holder, low and steady in the last of the wax. Zadi had the book on her knee under the table, one hand resting on it, not reading, just keeping it there.

Natalie sat back with her coffee. The steam came off it, leaned, and came off again. Amy said something low and Zadi laughed at it, and Natalie let the two of them go on, and drank her coffee while it was still warm, and stayed in her chair.

Amy's table had a card at every place, each one with a name on it in her small even handwriting, and Natalie found hers and sat where it told her to. She would never have thought to assign seats at her own table. Sitting down, she could see exactly why Amy had. Nobody hovered. Nobody did the little dance by the chairs, working out who went where and deferring and switching at the last second. Everyone came in, found a name, and sat.

"You made place cards," Zadi said, holding hers up.

"I made place cards," Amy said. "You're across from me so I can tell if you stop eating."

"I don't stop eating."

"I know. It's one of the things I like about you."

The kitchen was warm and very clean, the counters clear, everything that was not dinner already put away.

The soup came first, a squash soup that was better than Amy would admit it was. Zadi said so, at length. Amy told her the recipe was on a card in a box and she could have it if she wanted. Then came a plate of greens, then the main, each in its turn, because Amy had decided the order in advance.

A card stood propped on the sideboard with the whole meal on it top to bottom, like an itinerary, and every time a plate went out Natalie caught her checking it and going still a moment when the evening matched the card.

"Did you have a diagram," Zadi said. "For the seating. Tell me the truth."

"I had a diagram," Amy said, like it was the plainest thing in the world.

"I love that about you."

"You laugh every month," Amy said, "and then you eat in the right order and go home happy."

Zadi laughed. Natalie didn't, quite. She had spent a lot of years feeding people.

Natalie started to get up with her empty soup bowl, and Amy said, without turning from the counter, "Leave it."

"I'm right here. I can carry a bowl."

"Everything's handled. Sit down and be a guest." So Natalie sat and was a guest, and watched Amy run the dinner she had built. It was a strange thing, to sit with her hands empty while somebody else did the feeding. At her own table she was never still; here there was nothing to carry, because Amy had carried all of it already, in her head.

There were coasters, cork ones, squared up at every place. Natalie set her glass on hers and caught Amy clocking that she had, and the two of them let it pass without a word. By the door, on a low table, containers were already stacked with names taped to them, hers and Zadi's, the leftovers portioned out before the meal was half eaten.

The main was a chicken done with lemon, and it was good, and Natalie said so twice. Amy nodded and looked pleased and then asked if anyone wanted more before there wasn't any. The bread was good store bread, and when Zadi emptied the basket Amy brought out a second one she already had bagged on the counter. She had bought the spare when she did the shopping, in case the first ran out, and it had.

"This is the best I've eaten in weeks," Zadi said. "I've been living on toast and self-pity."

"I know about the toast," Amy said. "There's a container by the door with your name on it."

"How's the reading," Natalie said to Zadi, because she knew Zadi had run dry.

"It isn't," Zadi said. "I finished the blue one and nothing's caught me since. I've been rereading a cookbook for the pictures, which is a low place to be."

Amy said nothing to that. But when the plates were cleared — she cleared them, stacked and in order — she came back with a book and set it down by Zadi's coffee. "You said you had nothing," she said. "I saw this at the used place last week. I don't know if it's any good. It looked like you."

Zadi picked it up and turned it over and was quiet for a second. "Thank you," she said, in a smaller voice than the one she had been using all night.

The coffee came at the end, decaf, in cups Amy had set out before anyone arrived. On the sideboard the itinerary had come down to its last line, and then Natalie watched it come down to nothing — the main gone, the coffee poured, every item on the list met. Amy read the finished card, looked around for the next thing to do, and did not find one.

And then she sat down. She poured herself the last of the coffee and sat back with it. The talk kept going, looser now, off the plan and onto nothing much — the cold coming on, a neighbor's dog, whether the squash had been better than last year — and Amy put in a word here and there and mostly listened.

The card behind her was done, every line of it, and there was nothing left on it to do. Her coffee cooled at her elbow, forgotten. Outside, the sleet had come on, half rain and half snow, ticking at the dark glass, and none of them moved to go out into it yet.
